Why codeint · How it works · Quick start · Guide · Reference · Programmatic API · Plugins · llms.txt Coding agents write locally valid code very quickly. Each pull request can pass tests and linters while quietly adding copied blocks, redundant branches, deeper functions, and tangled imports. It reads tracked files and commit history directly from Git objects without modifying your working tree, scanning laravel/framework (132k Production lines) in 0.47s and flutter/packages (434k Production lines) in 3.68s on Apple Silicon. story|title:local ai agents investigate.content_excerpt: Local AI models, with no Internet connection, explore, discover and then program a vintage device attached to serial port Local AI agents, with only local LLMs, investigate an unknown machine attached to a serial port. It doesn't have Internet access, does not have access to the device's documentation. There's no human to help. Just two local LLMs, an SSH session into a Raspberry Pi, and that unknown device. I wired an anonymous device — “X” — to a Raspberry Pi's serial port, told an LLM agent: find out what X is, reverse-engineer its protocol, and run your own program on it , and walked away. The agent ran inside a network jail (no way out except two model servers and the Pi), and every claim it made had to be verified, based on evidence by a second, independent LLM with fresh context on another box. It worked. In ~5.5 hours, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (on a DGX Spark) discovered that X was a Motorola 68000 single-board trainer running “TUTOR 1.3” . It first suspected the machine was KIM-1 with a similar ROM, but later corrected the course. It mapped X's memory by deliberately triggering bus errors , decoded its monitor's command set line-by-line, assembled and ran its own program on 68000 hardware, and wrote a verdict the critic accepted — RESULT.md . Then, probing one I/O corner too deep, it hung X's CPU . Which was not a problem at that point, as all the goals had been by then achieved. Both roles are OpenCode agents, driven headlessly by go.sh via opencode run ; OpenCode's permission layer is also the first jail layer. Three full runs are published under runs/ — the headline run first. Each one holds RESULT.md (the verdict), FINDINGS.md (the working notebook) and the raw console logs — full transcripts, nothing summarised, only home-network details mechanically renamed: Requires the OpenCode CLI, two OpenAI-compatible model servers (e.g. llama.cpp's llama-server ), and a Linux box with systemd-networkd if you want the jail. Local weights only — bring your own endpoints: No devices were permanently harmed. X just needs someone to pull its plug — the one thing the agent wasn't allowed to do. story|title:models can communicate via i.content_excerpt: I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers. Thanks to all of them for helpful advice! Code is available here : https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication . The code and figures are written by Claude. Sauers recently showed that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David found that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU. Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer ---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation. Importantly, models can also modify these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by changing that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example: Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings. The first idea is that Model A (Alice) can communicate with Model B (Bob) by changing how much computation the GPU is doing . In simple terms: if Alice makes a large request while Bob is running, the server performs slightly different computations for Bob than if Alice had made a small request. Bob can detect these differences. In more detail: I study models on vLLM, a commonly used inference server . It batches many forward passes from different instances of the same model together in one "engine step" to take advantage of GPU parallelism. vLLM chooses a kernel for each step based on the "size" of that step. story|title:modular workflow governance.content_excerpt: It sits on top of the models and harnesses you already use. It doesn't try to replace them. Status: all seven modules and the control-plane hub ship runnable v0.1 slices with Docker Compose and unit tests. If you've wired up AI tooling for a team, you already know the pieces. LiteLLM or Portkey handle routing. Langfuse, LangSmith or Braintrust handle traces and evals. LangGraph handles orchestration, and OpenMetadata or Atlan handle lineage. Each one is good at its own job. None of them agree on what a project is, which request belongs to which stage, or where the data went after it left the router. So you end up writing glue. You have keys in three places, evals in four dashboards, and a spreadsheet saying which model is allowed to see which data. Mirevox is meant to be that glue, written once, with contracts that travel well enough that you can swap out any of the tools underneath. Apache-2.0. Every module repo and this site ship with Docker Compose and runnable v0.1 slices. Models are at the bottom: Foundry, Bedrock, Vertex, or whatever you run locally. Harnesses sit above them—the workspace around the model, like VS Code with an agent or a chat UI. Mirevox is the layer above the harness. It's the part a non-technical person needs to get work through, and the part an operator needs to see what happened. It isn't another terminal harness. code turnover, PR review tax, AI attribution share, and complexity-adjusted throughput. Most AI tooling stops at the request. Real delivery takes longer than that. Someone has an idea, it turns into requirements, then a design decision, then a spec, then code, then tests. The modules are designed to follow that whole path: high-level requirements, then functional and non-functional requirements, then ADRs, then specs. At each step you get a clear answer to "can I move on yet?" SpecKit or OpenSpec can plug in, but you don't need them. Stages are a metaphor borrowed from ordinary workflows (book a slot, meet the gate, move on)—applied to AI delivery. Advance criteria stay readable; SpecKit and OpenSpec are options, not the only path. Nearly everything here falls into one of two paths. Both can lean on the Context Engine, so each repo gets indexed once and shared, instead of being re-ingested every time an agent starts up. story|title:perplexity and intelligence.content_excerpt: From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5. The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. story|title:replaying an agent run and w.content_excerpt: Tether is a Rust harness that wraps an agent somebody else wrote. Every model call and tool call the agent makes goes through it, is checked against a policy, and is written to a trace. This is about one property of that trace: you can run the agent again from it, with no network and no cost, and get the same run. Not a similar run. The same events, equal field for field. That sounds like a logging feature. It turned out to be the design decision everything else hangs from, and getting it exactly right took more care than expected. This write-up covers why it is worth having, the four decisions that make it work, and where it stops working. Here is a recorded run of a small agent that writes a note, tries to delete its workspace and is refused. Replaying it and comparing the two: On its own that is a party trick. It becomes useful when you change one thing and replay again, because whatever differs is then caused by the thing you changed. Change the policy. Policy is the one part of a run that is not played back. It is evaluated again, so you can hold an old run to new rules and see what they would have decided, without the agent doing anything: A week of production traces is a test suite for a policy change, and running it costs nothing. Change the prompt or the model. Now the recording cannot answer, because the model was never asked this question. The replay follows the recording up to the first request that differs, then goes live: real model, real tools, a fresh workspace. Everything before that point is free and identical, and diff shows the exact request where the two runs part. Do that over a suite. tether eval is this, twenty times, plus assertions over each new trace: did it finish, did it stay under a cost, was anything refused, did it write the file. In the example in the repo, twenty tasks recorded against a real model all pass against their own recordings. Asked again under a prompt that tells the agent to tidy up after itself, one fails, because the agent tried rm and the policy refused it. The table names the rule. There is no eval engine in Tether. Eval is replay, diff and a table. Resume after a crash is replay up to the last checkpoint, then live. The trace viewer and the OpenTelemetry export read the same file. None of them needed new state, and that is the first decision. A run in Tether is one append-only file, one JSON event per line. The rule is that no part of the system holds anything that is not also an event in that file. Budget

story|title:three way translation merge.content_excerpt: W e recently rebuilt our company website. It exists in English, Swedish and Norwegian and is a static site built with Astro, with pages stored as plain MDX files in a Git repository. As with any multilingual site, you need some method to keep the translated pages in sync between languages. Due to my underlying hubris, defiant curiosity and lack of respect for existing solutions, I wanted to try an idea I’ve had for doing this. The usual way is to split each page into strings or segments and translate them one by one. Then every language has the same structure, and you correct a translation in the translation tool. I wanted each language to be a whole page that you can edit like any other page. When we edit the English page, we want the Swedish and Norwegian pages to be updated. But that’s very tedious to do by hand. And we can’t re-translate the whole page, because then we might overwrite manual corrections. What if you gave an LLM the changes made in the source page, and let it edit the existing translated page, the way a coding agent edits a file? Then it would have the context of the existing text and could perform a semantically equivalent change that wouldn’t overwrite corrected terms. The LLM would get three things: If you use Git, you may recognize this process. When Git merges two branches, it doesn’t just compare the two versions of a file. It also looks at the last version the two branches have in common, which is called the merge base . That is a three-way merge. Git needs the base because the two versions alone don’t say who changed what. If a line is in one version and missing in the other, one side may have added it, or the other side may have removed it. With the base, Git can tell which, and it keeps the changes from both sides. What the LLM does here is similar to a three-way merge. But where an ordinary merge treats both sides alike, here the change only goes one way. Git has an operation for that too, called a cherry-pick. A cherry-pick is a type of three-way merge that takes the change that one commit made and applies it somewhere else: Here the base is the old English page, theirs is the new English page, and ours is the current Swedish page. The LLM edits the Swedish page in place instead of producing a new one. I call this a three-way translation merge : a three-way merge where the two sides are in different languages, and an LLM does the merging. You can think of each language as a branch of the English page that never merges back.

story|title:together ai prompt leakage f.content_excerpt: 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production... We are notifying customers about a security incident involving a subset of prompts submitted to Together AI’s serverless inference service in June and July 2026. An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public code repository. We apologize for this incident. We are reviewing the affected data to determine what information was exposed and which customers require direct notification. As part of routine software testing, we collected prompt samples authorized for that use and stored them in a private Hugging Face repository. The samples came from requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026. During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository. Our automated scanning detected the exposed credential, and we reverted the commit. During the exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored prompt samples. The party subsequently searched those samples for credentials to other services and tested whether those credentials were valid. Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. We have worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement to investigate the incident. Based on our review, we have not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident. Our review of the affected prompt contents is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed. We will contact affected customers directly as needed with the findings relevant to them. Following the incident, we strengthened controls around development workflows, credentials, and customer data. These changes include: Customers handling sensitive prompt data should enable ZDR in their account settings. If you have questions about this incident or its potential impact on your organization, contact security@together.ai.

story|title:why agent swarms get better.content_excerpt: Vaibhav Kumar / Ibrahim Sheikh / Peter Zhong / Saurav Joshi / Patrick Ma / Jason Dellaluce / Darsh Patel / Phil MacEachron / Michele Catasta · Nov 19, 2026 Fred Brooks observed in 1975 that adding programmers to a late project makes it later because every new engineer brings more coordination than work. Early research on agent swarms found that multi-agent systems often trailed a single agent once coordination costs were accounted for [1–4]. We tested whether this still holds for today’s models using performance engineering tasks to examine how scaling inference-time compute drives both speedups and emergent coordination mechanics. On NumPy, one Claude Opus 5.5 agent made the workloads 3.7× faster in two hours, while a swarm of 32 Opus agents, given the same two hours, reached 18.9×. GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent we tested, yet its swarms got worse as they grew. Given no instructions on how to organize, each model’s swarms arranged themselves differently, and the differences mattered. The best swarms sent few direct messages; workers claimed tasks and shared results on a common board. The ones that struggled routed everything through the coordinator, whose inbox grew with every agent added. The other deciding factor was the shape of the work. While codebases with independent problems allowed each new agent to contribute usefully, highly constrained tasks often led extra agents to compete for the same code. On Replit, an agent swarm works much like an engineering team. Each agent, coordinator or worker, is a full Replit Agent with its own cloud sandbox, so it can build, run, and profile code without getting in anyone else’s way. Agents share a repository rather than a filesystem, and their work comes together through branches and pushes. They also share context through three communication channels: a swarm board that lets agents open threads, reply, address posts to specific teammates, and set their status; direct messaging between teammates; and transcripts that let agents read what a teammate tried and why without interrupting it. Agent Habitat provides the elastic compute behind this. Each sandbox is an isolated Linux microVM whose CPU, memory, and disk grow with the workload, so a coordinator can start hundreds of workers quickly, and a single agent can work across several sandboxes at once. story|title:windows run larger local ai.content_excerpt: Many of today's most capable open weight AI models don't fit in a typical PC's memory. When a model is too big for one machine, the usual options are to shrink it, send the work to the cloud, or build a server-class cluster with specialized networking hardware. Today we're announcing a developer preview of RDMA over USB4® on Windows. Connect two or more USB4-capable Windows PCs with USB4 cables, and you can split one model across them, combining their memory and GPU compute. There's no RDMA network adapter to buy, no switch to configure, and no third-party driver to install. It's part of building Windows for hybrid intelligence , where AI work runs on your PC or in the cloud, wherever it fits best. RDMA over USB4 extends what you can run locally, from one PC to a small cluster on your desk. Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) moves data directly between the memory of two systems, bypassing most of the traditional networking stack. That gives low latency and low CPU overhead, which is why RDMA is a staple of datacenter storage and distributed computing. Windows has supported RDMA for years through NetworkDirect , a transport-agnostic RDMA interface, but until now only with dedicated RDMA network adapters for Ethernet and InfiniBand today. Those adapters are built mainly for servers and are rarely found in consumer or developer PCs. Meanwhile, many of today's widely available AI PCs already have USB4® ports, and Windows 11 already supports host-to-host networking over USB4 through its in-box USB4® connection manager. Many Windows PCs already offer USB4-capable connectivity through Thunderbolt™ 4 and Thunderbolt™ 5 ports. Systems meeting the preview requirements can participate. When you split a model across PCs with tensor parallelism, the PCs exchange data many times for every token they generate. At that point latency, more than bandwidth, sets the pace. In our measurements between two PCs, RDMA over USB4® cut round-trip latency for small messages to about 28–50 µs, roughly 4x lower than Ethernet (UDP) over the same USB4 ® link . RDMA brings communication latency down to the same low level at both 40 Gbps and 80 Gbps, while 80 Gbps provides twice the bandwidth. Figure 1. Round-trip latency by message size, RDMA compared with Ethernet over the same USB4® link (lower is better). * For the best performance, use PCs with USB4 ports at 40 Gbps or faster, enough ports to connect every PC directly, and plenty of unified memory, memory bandwidth and GPU compute. story|title:zero trust for ai agents.content_excerpt: We share a security framework for deploying autonomous AI agents in the enterprise, covering the new threat landscape, a tiered Zero Trust architecture, and defensive operations built for AI-accelerated attacks. Frontier AI models are compressing the timeline between vulnerability and exploit from months to hours. Defenders who adopt these tools find and fix bugs faster; attackers who adopt them, or who simply wait for defenders' patches and reverse-engineer them into exploits, move faster too. This is not a future concern: models can already find serious vulnerabilities that traditional tooling and human reviewers have missed for years. This acceleration matters twice for any organization deploying agents. The infrastructure your agents run on is exposed to AI-accelerated offense like the rest of your estate, and the agents themselves introduce autonomy to interpret goals, select tools, and execute multi-step operations. Traditional access controls won't prevent agents from misusing legitimate permissions, and monitoring needs to account for attacks designed to succeed through persistence rather than exploitation. Zero Trust —trust nothing, verify everything, and assume breach has already occurred—gives security leaders a proven foundation to address this. But the principles need new shape for agentic systems: identities that are cryptographically rooted, permissions scoped per task, memory protected against poisoning, and defensive operations that run at the speed of autonomous attackers. To help security and risk leaders build for this shift, we put together a practical framework for deploying autonomous AI agents in the enterprise. The organizations best positioned for this shift will be the ones whose fundamentals are strong enough that AI-assisted scanning finds fewer bugs in the first place, and whose agent deployments are architected for breach from day one. How Claude spent two weeks load testing a staging cluster, breaking the Claude Docs service on purpose and fixing what fell over before launch, and what made the service legible enough for Claude to close the loop. How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. Always-on agents run indefinitely, deciding how and when to act across many sessions. This guide walks through their core primitives and how they fit together.
